EXTRA CLASS · KITCHEN HELPER

Welcome to the Kitchen.

The busiest room in the house, card by card: the everyday things a three-year-old already uses, the helper tools a four- or five-year-old can start with, the grown-up tools older kids love to name and the chef’s knife that teaches the kitchen’s biggest rule — knives are for grown-ups. Every tile below opens its own step-by-step lesson.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Little cooks, real tools, one big rule.

The Kitchen is a bonus class, kept beside the main learning path: the regular classes stay the core sequence, and this one is for families with a small cook at the counter. Thirty-five cards name the busiest room in the house, and every tile below opens its own step-by-step lesson — the tool, the job it does, the words to say and one thing to try at the real counter.

Every card carries an age pill, and the pills are the pacing: Ages 3 and up for the everyday things kids already use — the spoon, the fork, the plate, the mug, the bowl, the fridge; Ages 4–5 for the helper tools — the whisk, the rolling pin, the ladle, the measuring cups, the oven mitt; Ages 6 and up for the grown-up tools kids this age don’t use yet but love to name — the garlic press, the box grater, the mortar and pestle; and one card that is grown-ups only, the chef’s knife, which stays on the wall to teach the kitchen’s biggest rule. Nothing needs to be rushed — the pills do the pacing.

THE CLASS GAME

Kitchen Helper.

The class game is three steps: the child finds the item — in the drawer, on the counter, in the picture pile; says its name — out loud, proud, with the whole kitchen listening; then sorts the cards into two piles: I can use it and Grown-ups only. Every child’s piles are a little different, and the arguments are the best part — a four-year-old who claims the whisk but hands over the grater has just run the whole safety curriculum in one sitting.

Sorting by hand leads to sorting for real: the hot-check (which cards get HOT? drop a toy oven mitt on each — the kettle, the saucepan, the frying pan, the baking tray), the sharp check (peeler, grater, blender blades — grown-up tools, sharp and careful), and the mine pile that grows a real little cook. The card names the tool; the kitchen uses the tool; the recipe does the rest.

THE KITCHEN’S RULES, SAID OUT LOUD

Knives are for grown-ups. Hot means don’t touch.

Two rules live in this class, and they are taught out loud, kindly and often. Knives are for grown-ups — the chef’s knife stays on the card because hiding sharp things makes them fascinating, while naming them makes them understood; the child’s own tools are real: the butter knife, the board, the banana to slice. Hot means don’t touch — the kettle, the saucepan, the frying pan and the baking tray are the hot family, and every one of their lessons teaches the same sentence: hot, don’t touch, grown-ups only, step back. The rules are said every time, which is exactly how they stick.

And because rules without jobs get tested, every safety rule here comes with a job: the safety checker who announces the boiling kettle, the beep-watcher who calls the microwave, the safety caller who calls the sizzle. Small hands stay busy; the hot and sharp stay where they belong.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Baking Tray — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the baking tray as a two-state object: cool and fillable before the oven, untouchable after. The DING teaches the switch.

What is this?

A baking tray is the flat metal sheet cookies bake on — the same tray that goes in cool comes out hot, and knowing which state it is in IS kitchen safety.

What does it mean?

The tray is the clearest hot-things teacher because children see the state change with their own eyes: same shape, different temperature. Rules learned on a tray generalize to every oven thing.

What does the child need to know?

You need the tray, dough balls and the spacing lesson — "give each cookie room for its neighbour." The rule, said at every bake: "the tray is hot; we wait; grown-ups lift."

Why this matters

Tray burns are a classic little-kitchen injury, and they are preventable with one rehearsed sentence. Meanwhile the arranging job keeps small hands fully in the baking.

What it teaches

Spacing and estimation (dough spreads!), sequence awareness (fill, bake, WAIT, cool), and the rule-following that makes hot things boring instead of fascinating.

Words to learn

baking traydoughspreadhotwaitcool down

Say this to your child

“"Baking tray! Dough balls go on the tray — spaced apart, room to grow. Into the oven it slides… and when it comes out — HOT! We never touch the hot tray. Grown-ups lift it. We wait… and then we EAT!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the empty tray: "baking tray! The cookies’ bed."
  2. Fill together: dough balls with wide gaps — "each cookie needs room for its neighbour! They grow."
  3. Hand the tray to the oven (grown-up carries): "into the oven… twelve minutes!"
  4. The DING: "cookies are ready — and the tray is HOT. We wait. Grown-ups with oven mitts lift it."
  5. Watch the mitt parade to the cooling rack, repeat the rule, then — the best part — eat a cool one.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "baking tray" sit over a gray metal tray with raised edges — the tray as it waits, cool and empty, for its dough.

Ask your child

"What goes on the baking tray?" "Why do the dough balls need space?" "What do we say when the tray comes out?" (HOT — we wait!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might space dough with architect care, announce "HOT TRAY!" unprompted, or guard the cooling rack — the rule, self-enforcing.

Out in the real world

Trays come out of every oven: chips at grandma’s, pizza at home. The same sentence works at each one — "hot tray, we wait." One rule, whole life.

Try it together

Cookie Factory Line: trays of play-dough "cookies" get spaced, "baked" (counted to twelve), DINGED, and paraded to a toy cooling rack by mitt-wearing staff. Full production, zero burns.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do cookies bake?" (the tray) "Why do they need space?" (they spread) "What do we do when the DING comes?" (wait — hot!)

Staying safe

The tray is a hot family member: hot before it cools, untouchable until it does. The rule said every bake: hot tray — we wait, grown-ups lift. The wait is the job.

This lesson pairs with the Baking Tray flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Blender — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the blender from one safe step back: the child loads, announces and tastes — the grown-up owns the lid and the blades hidden underneath.

What is this?

A blender is the countertop machine that spins fruit into smoothies in twenty seconds — with the sharpest blades in the kitchen hidden at the bottom of its jug.

What does it mean?

The blender’s danger is invisible — blades under the jug, spinning too fast to see. "Lid on, blades are grown-ups’" said cheerfully at every smoothie is the whole protection.

What does the child need to know?

You need the blender, fruit and milk, and the division of labour: child loads, grown-up clicks the lid and presses the button, child announces the WHIRRR. Nobody touches the jug after — the grown-up pours.

Why this matters

A child who helped make the smoothie drinks the smoothie — the blender is the best anti-picky-eating machine ever built, and the ritual keeps it safe.

What it teaches

Sequence following, machine respect (not fear), the announcer job (language), and the fruit confidence that smoothies quietly build.

Words to learn

blenderfruitlidwhirrsmoothiepour

Say this to your child

“"Blender! Fruit goes in the jug — you load it! Lid on TIGHT — click. Press… WHIRRR! Everything spins into a smoothie! The blades are sharp and hidden — grown-ups pour. Now: the taste test!"”

Step by step

  1. Gather the fruit: "blender day! What goes in — banana? berries?" Child loads the jug.
  2. The lid: "grown-up clicks it TIGHT — the lid is the seatbelt!"
  3. The button: grown-up presses; the child is the announcer: "WHIRRR! It’s spinning!"
  4. Off, lid off by the grown-up only: "the blades live under there — sharp, sharp. Grown-ups handle the jug."
  5. Pour, serve, taste — and rate the smoothie. Tomorrow’s fruit list is already being written.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "blender" sits over a white countertop blender — jug on the base, the calm before the whirr.

Ask your child

"What goes in the blender?" "Who clicks the lid?" (grown-ups) "What do we say when it spins?" (WHIRRR!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might announce every whirr like a rocket launch, load tomorrow’s fruit unprompted, or refuse to drink anything NOT blended — power and produce, together.

Out in the real world

Smoothies happen at cafés, markets, grandma’s. Each whirr from another kitchen is a name-check: "a blender — like ours!" The rule rides along.

Try it together

Smoothie Bar: menus drawn, orders taken (teddies welcome), one blended "smoothie" (milkshake or yogurt blend) per round. The announcer job rotates — everyone gets a WHIRRR.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who clicks the lid?" (grown-ups) "Where do the blades live?" (under the jug — sharp!) "What does the blender say?" (WHIRRR!)

Staying safe

The blender hides the kitchen’s sharpest blades — under the jug, spinning too fast to see. Rule: lid on tight, blades and jug are grown-ups’, the child loads, announces and tastes.

This lesson pairs with the Blender flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Box Grater — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the box grater as a look-and-learn tool: count the sides, compare the holes, watch the shred — and learn that the friendliest-looking tool is sharp.

What is this?

A box grater is the tall four-sided shredder — big holes for ribbons, small holes for dust, and every edge sharp enough to earn respect.

What does it mean?

The grater looks friendly and behaves sharp — which is exactly why it is the great sharp-things teacher. Learning "the holes are blades" by LOOKING, at six, prevents the finger scrape at nine.

What does the child need to know?

You need the grater, a block of cheese and flat-palm demo technique: "palm flat on top, fingers FAR away." The child’s job: count the sides, compare the holes, eat the results.

Why this matters

Graters cause more little-finger scrapes than knives — and this card is the antidote. Respect taught early, without fear, on a tool that means well.

What it teaches

Observation (hole sizes, four faces), tool respect, the flat-palm technique (watched now, used years later), and cheese confidence.

Words to learn

box gratersidesholessharpshredcareful

Say this to your child

“"Box grater! The four-sided tower. Big holes for ribbons of cheese, small holes for cheese snow. Careful — the holes are SHARP! We look with our eyes. Watch: flat palm, fingers far away… SHRED!"”

Step by step

  1. Meet the tower: "box grater! Count the sides — one, two, three, four!"
  2. Compare the holes: "big holes — big shreds. Small holes — tiny snow." Match hole to result at the demo.
  3. The demo, flat palm: grown-up shreds — "watch my hand: flat on top, fingers FAR away."
  4. Say the rule together: "the holes are SHARP — we look with our eyes, not our fingers."
  5. Sprinkle the shreds on pasta and eat — respect taught, dinner served.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "box grater" sit over a green and white four-sided grater — every face shown, every hole a small sharp promise.

Ask your child

"How many sides does the grater have?" (four) "Which holes make big shreds?" "What do we do with sharp things?" (look — grown-ups use)

What your child can say or do

Your child might count the sides daily, request "cheese snow!" on everything, or recite the rule at the drawer — respect, installed.

Out in the real world

Graters appear at pizza nights, taco bars, grandma’s kitchen. Each one gets the same nod: "sharp tower — grown-ups shred." The rule travels by name.

Try it together

Grater Gallery: sort cheese shreds by hole size onto a plate — ribbons, strips, snow. The artist signs the work with a sprinkle. Then pasta for everyone.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many sides?" (four) "Are the holes sharp?" (yes — very!) "What do we use on the grater?" (our eyes!)

Staying safe

Every hole on a grater is a small blade — graters scrape more little fingers than knives do. Rule: sharp things are grown-up things; the child counts sides, compares holes and eats the results.

This lesson pairs with the Box Grater flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Chef’s Knife — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the chef’s knife by teaching the rule: knives are for grown-ups. Named, respected, never hidden — and matched with the real tools the child DOES own.

What is this?

A chef’s knife is the kitchen’s sharpest, biggest knife — the one that does the serious chopping — and the one tool in this set that is not for children at any age here.

What does it mean?

Hiding sharp things makes them fascinating; naming them makes them understood. The rule said kindly and repeatedly — "knives are for grown-ups" — builds respect without fear.

What does the child need to know?

You need the drawer where the knife lives and the same sentence every time it comes out. Then the counter-offer: the child’s own tools — butter knife, board, banana to slice. Helping never stops; it uses the right tools.

Why this matters

A child who knows the rule, the reason and their own safe tools is the safest child in the kitchen. The ban is small; the safety system around it is generous.

What it teaches

Rule internalisation (the child says it first), tool taxonomy (mine vs grown-ups’), and the patience of a cook-in-training who knows their path forward.

Words to learn

chef’s knifesharpgrown-upsrulebutter knifesomeday

Say this to your child

“"Chef’s knife! The big, sharp knife. Here is the kitchen’s biggest rule: KNIVES ARE FOR GROWN-UPS. Your tools are the butter knife and the board — and they are real tools, too. Watch: banana coins! The chef’s knife waits for big hands, years from now."”

Step by step

  1. At the drawer, name it plainly: "chef’s knife — the big, sharp one."
  2. The rule, same words every time: "KNIVES ARE FOR GROWN-UPS. Not today, not with help — grown-ups only."
  3. Give the why: "the knife is a great tool — and it is sharp enough to need big, trained hands. Yours are growing."
  4. The counter-offer, same lesson: "YOUR tools: the butter knife, the board, the banana. Watch!" — and slice.
  5. Return the knife together, drawer closed, rule repeated by the child if they will. Lesson done in ninety seconds, working for years.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "chef’s knife" sit over a long blade with a black handle — shown plainly, never hidden, because named things are respected things.

Ask your child

"Who uses the chef’s knife?" (grown-ups) "What are YOUR tools?" (butter knife, board) "Why do knives wait?" (sharp — big trained hands)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say the rule at the drawer unprompted, or announce "knives are for grown-ups!" to a visiting cousin — the household’s safety officer, elected.

Out in the real world

Knives appear in every kitchen on Earth, and the rule travels with the child — grandma’s, the holiday flat, the friend’s house. One sentence, portable safety.

Try it together

Tool Sort: kitchen tools face-up on the table — "mine" pile and "grown-ups’" pile. The butter knife and whisk land in MY pile; the chef’s knife rules its own. Sorting IS the safety lesson.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who uses knives?" (grown-ups) "What is YOUR slicing tool?" (the butter knife) "Say the biggest rule…" (knives are for grown-ups!)

Staying safe

The owner’s rule, taught straight: knives are for grown-ups. The knife stays on the card so the rule can be taught, not hidden — and the child’s own tools (butter knife, board, soft food) keep the helping alive.

This lesson pairs with the Chef’s Knife flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Coffee Maker — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the coffee maker as the kitchen’s most familiar hands-off machine: it hums, it drips, and the child’s job is to let it work — while owning the cold drinks.

What is this?

A coffee maker drips hot water through coffee grounds into a glass jug, and its plate keeps the jug hot all morning. Hot machine, hot jug — a look-and-learn member of the hot family.

What does it mean?

The coffee maker is a low-drama place to rehearse the hot rule: nothing about it invites touch. Children learn that some machines are watched, named and left alone — a whole category of safety in one appliance.

What does the child need to know?

You need the machine and the brew ritual, watched from outside: water in, filter in, button on — "drip, drip, drip." The rule: "the jug is hot; grown-ups pour." The counter-offer: your child pours the COLD drinks.

Why this matters

A child with a real pouring job (juice! water!) stays in the serving business safely, while the hot rule lands where it belongs — on the machine that is genuinely hot.

What it teaches

Machine-watching patience, the hot-rule rehearsal, pouring control (cold side), and the family-roles picture: who runs which machine.

Words to learn

coffee makerdripfilterjughotpour

Say this to your child

“"Coffee maker! Drip, drip, drip — the morning machine. Water in, coffee in… the jug fills up. The jug is HOT — grown-ups only. And YOUR job: the cold drinks! Juice for everyone — pour with two hands!"”

Step by step

  1. Name the machine: "coffee maker! The morning machine."
  2. Watch a brew from the outside: "water in the top… coffee in the filter… button — drip, drip, drip!"
  3. The rule while it drips: "the jug gets HOT. The coffee maker is a grown-up machine — we watch."
  4. The counter-offer at the fridge: "YOUR pouring job — the cold drinks! Juice for the table… water for the cups."
  5. Pour and serve. Two pouring jobs, two temperatures, one safe system.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "coffee maker" sit over a drip machine with its glass jug — the jug about to fill, drop by patient drop.

Ask your child

"What does the coffee maker do?" (drips) "Who pours the coffee?" (grown-ups — the jug is hot) "What is YOUR pouring job?" (the cold drinks)

What your child can say or do

Your child might narrate every drip, referee the jug from afar ("HOT!"), or pour juice for the whole table — both jobs, both temperatures.

Out in the real world

Coffee machines hum in every kitchen and hotel. Each brew is a free rehearsal: "dripping… the jug is hot… my job is the juice." Roles confirmed, everywhere.

Try it together

Family Café: the cold-drink station is the child’s — jug of juice, cups, two-hand pouring, orders taken. The coffee maker hums in the background, officially out of bounds and therefore uninteresting.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the coffee maker make?" (coffee) "Is the jug hot?" (yes — all morning) "What do YOU pour?" (cold drinks!)

Staying safe

The jug and the plate under it stay hot for hours — long after the drip stops. Rule: the coffee maker is a grown-up machine, watched and named; the child owns the cold-drink pouring.

This lesson pairs with the Coffee Maker flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

Colander — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the colander through its two jobs — washing fruit and draining pasta — with the water-vanishing trick that makes the holes unforgettable.

What is this?

A colander is the bowl full of holes: water runs through, food stays in. It washes berries and drains pasta, and it answers its own mystery — where does the water go?

What does it mean?

The colander teaches filtering: let the liquid pass, keep the solid. The same idea returns in sieves, strainers and tea bags for the rest of life — learned here over grapes.

What does the child need to know?

You need the colander, grapes or berries, and a tap the child can work. The pasta drain is the grand demo — grown-up carries the hot pot, child holds the colander steady.

Why this matters

Fruit washing is a zero-risk job with a delicious result, and pasta draining is the kitchen’s favourite magic trick. Both live in one holey bowl.

What it teaches

Tap control, gentle shaking (draining), cause and effect (holes lose water, keep food), and the fruit-washing hygiene habit.

Words to learn

colanderholeswashdrainwaterthrough

Say this to your child

“"Colander! The holey bowl. Grapes in — water on — the water runs THROUGH the holes and the grapes stay in! And on pasta night: WHOOSH — the pasta water vanishes! Holes that hold food and lose water. Magic — but it is just holes."”

Step by step

  1. Show the holes: "colander! A bowl FULL of holes — look through it!"
  2. The wash: "grapes in… water on… woosh!" The child works the tap and watches water thread through.
  3. The question: "where did the water GO?" (through the holes!) "Where are the grapes?" (still in!)
  4. The grand demo: pasta night, colander in the sink held steady by the child, hot pot carried by the grown-up — "pour… WHOOSH! The water goes through. The pasta stays!"
  5. Shake gently to drain: "little shakes… the last drips leave. Dinner is served."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "colander" sits over a green colander, its drain holes dotted across every side — the water’s exits, drawn in dots.

Ask your child

"What do the holes do?" (let water through) "Where are the grapes after washing?" (still in the colander) "What does the colander do on pasta night?" (drains!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might inspect every hole, wash everything in the fruit bowl, or hold the colander on pasta night with two hands and total gravity — filtering, owned.

Out in the real world

Colanders hang in kitchens everywhere and pool-side caddies too. Any perforated bowl becomes a demo: "holes — like your colander!"

Try it together

Sieve Science: colander vs plate — pour water on both, which holds? Then sand through the colander at the sandbox: what stays, what falls? Filtering, tested twice.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a colander do?" (drains water) "What stays in?" (the food) "Where does the water go?" (through the holes!)

This lesson pairs with the Colander flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Cooking Spoon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the cooking spoon in two promotions: first the dry-bowl practice where stirring is free, then the real batter where the stir becomes the child’s signature.

What is this?

A cooking spoon is the big wooden spoon that stirs everything — blunt, strong and the classic first tool of every little helper.

What does it mean?

Stirring is grip, wrist control and patience in one motion. The wooden spoon earns its place because it cannot cut, cannot scratch and forgives every enthusiastic swirl.

What does the child need to know?

You need the spoon, a bowl of dry oats for practice and one promotion to real batter when the circles are steady. The script: "round and round — you are the stirrer!"

Why this matters

A dry bowl lets the wrist learn without waste: no spills, no eggs harmed, endless reps. When the real batter comes, the stir arrives already trained.

What it teaches

Wrist rotation and control, two-hand option for heavy batter, stir-while-holding-the-bowl coordination, and recipe stamina.

Words to learn

cooking spoonstirround and roundbatterwristmix

Say this to your child

“"Cooking spoon! Hold it like a paddle. Round and round — stir the oats! Fast circles… slow circles… now the REAL batter — you stir! Look at that: smooth, no lumps. You are the stirrer today. Spoon-licking rights are yours."”

Step by step

  1. Meet the spoon: "cooking spoon! The wooden stirrer — hold it like a paddle."
  2. The practice bowl: dry oats — "stir! Round and round… fast circles… slow circles… figure eights!" Free reps, zero mess.
  3. The graduation: real batter, bowl held steady by the grown-up or a damp cloth — "your stir now!"
  4. Narrate the result: "look — no lumps! Your stirring did that."
  5. Lick-the-spoon rights: the stirrer tastes first. Tradition, earned.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "cooking spoon" sit over a wooden spoon — plain, sturdy and slightly worn from a thousand stirs.

Ask your child

"What does the spoon do?" (stirs!) "Show me fast circles… slow circles." "Who licks the spoon?" (the stirrer!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might stir everything (soup, bath, air), demand stirrer status on every bake, or teach a teddy to stir — the tool, beloved.

Out in the real world

Wooden spoons rest in every kitchen drawer on Earth. Each one is a handshake waiting: "that is a cooking spoon — like yours!"

Try it together

Stir-a-Pot Band: pots and spoons as a rhythm section (soft taps only), then the switch to real stirring — music and cooking, one drawer apart.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the spoon do?" (stirs) "Show me round and round!" "What did your stirring make?" (smooth batter!)

This lesson pairs with the Cooking Spoon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Cutting Board — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the cutting board as the chopping address: food ON the board, butter knife in hand, soft food first — real slicing, safely begun.

What is this?

A cutting board is the flat wooden stage where chopping happens — it holds the food still and keeps the counter (and the fingers) safe.

What does it mean?

The board card teaches a rule and a skill together: chopping happens on the board, never in the hand — and soft foods get the butter knife. This is the on-ramp to every knife skill to come.

What does the child need to know?

You need the board, a butter knife and a banana. The script: "the banana lives ON the board… the butter knife cuts… fingers on top, away from the blade." Coins for cereal, pride for the cook.

Why this matters

Real slicing jobs with safe tools are how young cooks earn their way toward bigger knives — years later, on a board just like this one. The path starts with a banana.

What it teaches

Two-hand coordination (hold and slice), the sawing motion, safe knife habits from day one, and snack independence — the sliced banana disappears.

Words to learn

cutting boardbutter knifeslicecoinssoftsteady

Say this to your child

“"Cutting board! The banana goes ON the board — never chop without it. Your butter knife… saw, saw… a banana coin! Again! Fingers on top of the banana, away from the blade. You are really slicing!"”

Step by step

  1. Stage the board: "cutting board! The chopping spot — food lives ON it."
  2. Butter knife briefing: "your knife — it cuts soft food. The sharp knives wait for big hands."
  3. The first slice: banana on the board, one hand steadying on TOP — "saw… saw… a coin!"
  4. The pile grows: coins for cereal, for pancakes, for eating straight off the board (quality control).
  5. The tidy: crumbs to the bin, board wiped, knife to the sink — the chef closes the kitchen.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "cutting board" sit over a wooden board with its handle hole — flat, worn and ready for its first banana.

Ask your child

"Where does chopping happen?" (on the board) "What does the butter knife cut?" (soft food) "Where do fingers go?" (on top, away from the blade)

What your child can say or do

Your child might slice every soft fruit in the house, serve banana coins at breakfast, or correct a visitor: "the board first!" — the rule, owned.

Out in the real world

Boards appear at every real knife moment: the chopping at the market stall, the carving at Christmas. "A cutting board — the chopping spot!" scales up with the cook.

Try it together

Snack Bar: a board, a butter knife, a bowl of soft fruit — the child runs the snack bar, slicing and serving. Payment accepted in bites and thank-yous.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does food go for chopping?" (on the board) "What cuts the banana?" (the butter knife) "Where do fingers stay?" (on top, safe)

Staying safe

The board is where knife safety begins: chopping on the board, never in the hand; the butter knife for soft food only; the sharp knives are grown-ups’. Habits learned here are the ones that last.

This lesson pairs with the Cutting Board flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Dishwasher — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the dishwasher as the first chore machine: loading the cutlery basket is matching practice that ends with a machine full of clean dishes.

What is this?

A dishwasher is the machine under the counter that washes the dishes — no flame, no blade, no reachable heat: the gentlest appliance in the kitchen, and the natural first-chore machine.

What does it mean?

Loading cutlery is sorting with a purpose: every spoon has a spot, every plate a slot. The child learns one-to-one matching, care and the big idea that everyone’s dishes get washed together.

What does the child need to know?

You need the cutlery basket and the family rule (spoons up or down — pick one, keep it). One item at a time, into its spot. Unloading cups to the low shelf is the promotion, later.

Why this matters

The dishwasher’s gentleness is exactly why it comes first: a chore with zero danger that still delivers the full satisfaction of a real job done.

What it teaches

Sorting and one-to-one matching, care with others’ things, chore persistence, and the machine-as-helper idea (the family has robots!).

Words to learn

dishwasherbasketspoonsslotswashunload

Say this to your child

“"Dishwasher! The dishes ride inside. Spoons in their spots — one, two, three! Forks, plates, cups… click the door — WHOOSH, wash wash wash! And tomorrow: clean! Your job: the spoons — and the cups when they are clean."”

Step by step

  1. Open the machine together: "dishwasher! The dish-washing machine."
  2. The basket job: "spoons in their spots — one at a time!" (Family rule stated once, kept forever.)
  3. Sort and load: knives and forks by the grown-up or alongside, spoons by the handful of one.
  4. The close: "click the door… press START… whoosh, wash wash wash!"
  5. The promotion, next day: "they are clean! Cups to the low shelf — unload!" The full cycle, owned.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "dishwasher" sits over a white built-in machine — the door shut, the panel waiting for its button.

Ask your child

"What does the dishwasher do?" (washes the dishes) "Where do the spoons go?" (their spots in the basket) "What happens after the whoosh?" (clean dishes — unload!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might sort the whole basket unprompted, press START with ceremony, or unload cups to their shelf without being asked — chore pride, banked.

Out in the real world

Dishwashers hum in kitchens everywhere — and hotels, and holiday flats. Same machine, same job: "spoons in their spots" travels with the child.

Try it together

Dish Café: after a toy tea party, EVERY cup gets loaded — basket sorted, door clicked, whoosh announced. The café has standards; the dishwasher has a colleague.

Understanding check

Ask: "What washes the dishes?" (the dishwasher) "Whose job is the spoon basket?" (mine!) "What comes after the whoosh?" (clean — unload!)

This lesson pairs with the Dishwasher flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Food Thermometer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the food thermometer as kitchen science: temperature is invisible, but a number makes it visible — and the number tells the truth about dinner.

What is this?

A food thermometer is the thin probe with the digital screen that checks the INSIDE of the food — how cooks know dinner is properly cooked, not just looking cooked.

What does it mean?

This is a name-and-watch card: the child reads the number and learns the big idea — cooks measure. The outside can lie; the inside number cannot.

What does the child need to know?

You need a roast, soup or anything worth checking. Grown-up runs the probe, child reads the screen: "what does the number say? Is it big enough?"

Why this matters

The checking habit is the deepest lesson on the Ages 6+ shelf: the best cooks measure. Someday the child will own a thermometer; today they own its name and job.

What it teaches

Number reading with a purpose, the inside-vs-outside idea, kitchen-science curiosity, and safety thinking: proper temperature is how food stays safe.

Words to learn

food thermometerprobetemperaturenumbercookedcheck

Say this to your child

“"Food thermometer! The pointy end goes in the food… and the screen shows a number — how hot the INSIDE is. Read it to me! When the number is big enough, the food is properly cooked. Cooks always check."”

Step by step

  1. Meet the tool: "food thermometer! The temperature checker — science you can eat."
  2. The demo: grown-up inserts the probe into the thickest part — "the screen shows a NUMBER."
  3. Child reads it aloud: "what does it say?"
  4. The big idea: "the OUTSIDE can look cooked while the inside is not. The number tells the truth. When the number is high enough — dinner is really ready."
  5. The retirement: probe out (grown-up), dinner served, the child announces: "checked and ready!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "food thermometer" sit over a digital probe thermometer — needle-thin, screen ready, waiting to tell the truth.

Ask your child

"What does the thermometer check?" (the inside temperature) "Who runs the probe?" (grown-ups) "What does the number tell us?" (if the food is really cooked)

What your child can say or do

Your child might read every number aloud, ask "is the inside cooked?" at every meal, or announce "checked!" — measurement, adopted.

Out in the real world

Thermometers hide in plain sight: the fridge dial, the oven display, the fever checker. Same idea — numbers that keep us safe — met at dinner.

Try it together

Temperature Lab: hot water, warm water, cold water — probe each (grown-up hands) and read the three numbers. The child orders them: hottest, middle, coldest. Science, served.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the thermometer check?" (the inside) "Can the outside lie?" (yes!) "Who reads the number?" (me!)

Staying safe

The probe is pointy and the food is hot: grown-ups handle the thermometer end to end. The child’s job is reading the number — the safest and most important seat in the lab.

This lesson pairs with the Food Thermometer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Fork — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the fork on easy wins: banana coins, soft potato, melon cubes — push, lift, eat — until the four little teeth do the work fingers used to.

What is this?

A fork is the spiky tool with four tines that spears food for eating — the workhorse of every meal and a genuine fine-motor milestone.

What does it mean?

Fork control is aim, push, lift and steady — real hand skills. It also marks the move from finger food to table food: a small step with a large side order of pride.

What does the child need to know?

You need a child-size fork with a fat handle and the easiest targets first: banana coins, potato cubes, melon. The script: "push… lift… and EAT!" The stab-and-twist comes later.

Why this matters

A child who feeds themselves with a fork eats more, messes less and sits longer. The tool does the teaching; the cubed fruit does the motivating.

What it teaches

Aim and push control, lift-and-steady coordination, hand-to-mouth precision, and table-manners seeds (fork rests between bites).

Words to learn

forktinespushliftspeareat

Say this to your child

“"Fork! Four little teeth. Hold it like a flag… push into the banana… LIFT… and EAT! You did it with a fork! Again — push, lift, eat. The fork does what your fingers used to — big kid tools!"”

Step by step

  1. Meet the teeth: "fork! Four little teeth — count them!"
  2. The grip: fist first, that is correct for now — "hold it like a flag."
  3. Easy targets: "push into the banana… LIFT… and eat!" First spears deserve applause.
  4. The wobble zone: misses happen — "the banana escaped! Chase it again." Humour keeps the reps coming.
  5. The upgrade: two foods on one fork — a double spear! Then the restful pose: fork down between bites. Table set, child promoted.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "fork" sits over a fork with a green handle, four tines up — the tool, presented like cutlery to a guest of honour.

Ask your child

"How many teeth does a fork have?" (four) "Show me push and lift!" "What did your fork spear today?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might spear everything on the plate (peas are the boss level), or ask for "the sharp spoon" — the tool, claimed by appetite.

Out in the real world

Forks set every table: picnics, restaurants, grandma’s best set. Each place setting is a practice invitation — "your fork, sir!"

Try it together

Fork Gym: a plate of soft cubes, a timer-free course — spear five, rest, spear five more. Medal ceremony optional; full tummy guaranteed.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a fork do?" (spears food) "Show me push… lift!" "Which food was easy? Which was tricky?" — grip, spear, eat: the tool is working.

This lesson pairs with the Fork flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Frying Pan — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the frying pan by splitting the job: the pan sizzles untouched, the child cracks and whisks at the counter — hot and helpful, each in their place.

What is this?

A frying pan is the black pan that makes the sizzle — eggs, pancakes, bacon — and, like everything on the stove, a firm member of the hot, don’t-touch family.

What does it mean?

The pan’s spitting oil makes it the most jump-worthy hot thing in the kitchen — so the rule is said early and often. Meanwhile the crack-an-egg job keeps little hands fully in the cooking.

What does the child need to know?

You need the counter (the child’s station) and the pan (the grown-up’s). The safety call is a job: "sizzling means step back!" — said BY the child, every time.

Why this matters

Separation of hot and helpful is the whole trick of cooking with kids: the pan does the reaching, the child does everything else — and never feels shut out.

What it teaches

Egg-cracking technique (two hands, one confident tap), whisking, the safety-call habit, and the sound vocabulary: sizzle, crack, whish.

Words to learn

frying pansizzlehotoilcrackstep back

Say this to your child

“"Frying pan! Sizzle sizzle — the pan is cooking. The pan is HOT and the oil jumps — when you hear the sizzle, step back! You crack the eggs at the counter: tap… pull… plop! Whisk whisk. The pan sizzles, the team cooks."”

Step by step

  1. Name the sound: "frying pan! Listen — sizzle sizzle. That is cooking happening."
  2. The rule, with a job: "the pan is HOT and the oil jumps. When you hear the sizzle — step back! You are the safety caller."
  3. The child’s station at the counter: eggs cracked — "one confident tap… both thumbs… PULL!"
  4. Whisk the eggs; the grown-up works the pan. The sizzle arrives; the safety caller announces it.
  5. Serve: "eggs — cracked by you, sizzled by the pan. TEAM!" Breakfast has a credits roll.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "frying pan" sit over a black pan with a green handle — flat, glossy and always one second away from the sizzle.

Ask your child

"What does the frying pan say?" (sizzle sizzle!) "What do we do when it sizzles?" (step back!) "What was YOUR job?" (crack and whisk!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might referee every sizzle, crack eggs with both thumbs and ceremony, or request "the sizzle eggs" by name — the team, unbroken.

Out in the real world

Sizzles announce themselves: the market stall, the café kitchen, grandma’s breakfast. Each one is a cue: "sizzling — step back!" The rule hears it first.

Try it together

Toy Sizzle: a play pan "cooks" pompom eggs while the safety caller patrols — "sizzle! Step back!" The rule rehearsed at toy scale keeps the real pan’s rule loud.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the pan say when it cooks?" (sizzle!) "What do we do?" (step back!) "Where do the eggs get cracked?" (at the counter — by me!)

Staying safe

The frying pan’s oil spits, and the pan itself is the hottest thing on the stove. Rule: the pan is grown-ups’ — the child’s stations are cracking, whisking and the safety call. Turn pan handles inward.

This lesson pairs with the Frying Pan flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Funnel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the funnel as engineering in one word: change a wide pour into a narrow stream — demonstrated with water, and with one glorious puddle where puddles are allowed.

What is this?

A funnel is the little cone that guides a pour into a small opening — water, oil, juice, all delivered neatly into bottles that would otherwise splash.

What does it mean?

This is a name-and-try card: the concept — guiding flow — is the point more than the tool. A child who explains WHY the funnel works has discovered fluid dynamics at the sink.

What does the child need to know?

You need the funnel, an empty bottle, a jug of water — and outdoor permission for the control experiment (no funnel, full pour, one puddle).

Why this matters

Cause and effect is unforgettable when one version is neat and the other is a puddle. The funnel demo delivers both in under a minute.

What it teaches

Pouring control, guided-flow thinking, the wide-vs-narrow concept, and tidy-up reflexes (the puddle demo is outdoors for a reason).

Words to learn

funnelconepourstreambottleno spills

Say this to your child

“"Funnel! Stand it in the bottle… pour — the water runs down the cone, right into the bottle! No spills, no puddles. And with NO funnel? (Outside!) — SPLASH! Now you know: the funnel makes wide pours neat."”

Step by step

  1. Meet the cone: "funnel! Wide at the top, narrow at the bottom — watch what it does."
  2. The neat demo: funnel in the bottle mouth, child pours from the jug — "the water glides… right in! Zero puddles."
  3. The control experiment (outside): same jug, NO funnel, full tilt — "the puddle! That is why the funnel exists."
  4. The why, asked back: "what does the funnel do?" (makes the opening wide, the stream narrow)
  5. The encore: funnel a scoop of rice into a jar — solids work too. The tool has range.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "funnel" sits over a gray and green cone — wide mouth up, narrow stem down, the whole trick in its shape.

Ask your child

"What does the funnel do?" (guides the pour) "What happens with NO funnel?" (a puddle!) "What else could we funnel?" (rice! sand! juice!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might funnel everything pourable, narrate "wide in, narrow out!", or request the puddle demo weekly — flow, mastered.

Out in the real world

Funnels hide in garages (oil), petrol stations and craft drawers. Each sighting gets the nod: "a funnel — the pouring helper." The concept scales to hoses and funnels forever.

Try it together

Water Lab: funnels of different sizes, bottles of different necks — which pair pours fastest? Test, time, repeat. The lab is open; the floor is waterproof.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the funnel do?" (guides pours) "Why is it wide at the top?" (to catch the pour) "What did we learn outside?" (no funnel = puddle!)

This lesson pairs with the Funnel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Garlic Press — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the garlic press as a mechanism to admire: a clove goes in, both handles squeeze, tiny garlic comes out the holes — smelly, strong and delicious.

What is this?

A garlic press is the green squeezer that crushes a clove into mince in one squeeze — a lever machine with a little basket and a wall of tiny holes.

What does it mean?

The Ages 6+ cards are what-is-this cards: named, explored, understood — not yet used. The press is a favourite because its mechanism is visible: squeeze here, mince there.

What does the child need to know?

You need the press, a garlic clove and a grown-up’s hands over the child’s for the squeeze. The smell afterwards is the party trick.

Why this matters

Tools whose mechanism can be SEEN (lever! holes! pressure!) teach how machines think. The press is a lever lesson that ends in spaghetti sauce.

What it teaches

Mechanical thinking (lever, pressure, holes), sensory vocabulary (smell!), and the future-cook promise: "you’ll use one someday."

Words to learn

garlic pressclovesqueezeminceholeslever

Say this to your child

“"Garlic press! A clove goes in the basket… SQUEEZE both handles… and out comes tiny garlic through the holes! Smell it — strong and delicious! It is a lever machine. You will use one someday — today, you know its trick."”

Step by step

  1. Meet the machine: "garlic press! The squeezer — look at the little basket and the tiny holes."
  2. Open and close the handles: "it is a LEVER — squeeze here, press there."
  3. The demo, hands together: clove in the basket… "SQUEEZE!"… open — "tiny garlic through the holes!"
  4. The smell test: "sniff! THAT is garlic. Strong, isn’t it?"
  5. The promise: "one day, big hands, your squeeze. Today you know its name and its trick."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "garlic press" sit over a green press with two handles and a basket of holes — the mechanism, visible and waiting.

Ask your child

"What goes in the basket?" (a garlic clove) "What do we do?" (squeeze!) "What comes out the holes?" (tiny garlic!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might squeeze air enthusiastically, smell everything garlic-adjacent, or request "the squeezer" for spaghetti night — mechanism, adored.

Out in the real world

Garlic presses squeeze in kitchens worldwide — and the lever idea repeats in nutcrackers, staplers and car jacks. One press, a family of machines.

Try it together

Lever Hunt: find the house’s squeezers and pressers — nutcracker, peg, stapler (grown-up hands). "Same trick as the garlic press!" Machines, reunited.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the press do?" (minces garlic) "What kind of machine is it?" (a lever!) "What comes out the holes?" (tiny garlic!)

This lesson pairs with the Garlic Press flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Kettle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the kettle as the kitchen’s loudest safety teacher: it whistles, it steams, and the rule said beside it — hot, don’t touch — generalizes to every hot thing after.

What is this?

A kettle is the stovetop pot that boils water for tea and cocoa — the loudest, steamiest member of the hot family, and the first hot thing most children learn to name.

What does it mean?

The kettle teaches a pattern, not just a rule: hot things announce themselves (whistle, steam, glow), and the response is always the same — hands back, step back, grown-ups only.

What does the child need to know?

You need the kettle (on when possible, named either way) and the safety pose: hands clasped behind the back, one big step back. The child’s job: safety checker — "the kettle is HOT!"

Why this matters

A child who learns "the kettle is hot, I step back" owns the pattern for the saucepan, the oven door, the BBQ — the rule generalizes for free.

What it teaches

Rule internalisation, body control (the pose), sound-association (whistle = hot), and the dignity of a job that keeps people safe.

Words to learn

kettleboilsteamhotstep backsafety checker

Say this to your child

“"Kettle! It boils the water — very, VERY hot. Hot, don’t touch — grown-ups only! Show me the safety pose… hands back, step back! When the kettle whistles, you are the safety checker: THE KETTLE IS HOT!"”

Step by step

  1. Name the machine: "kettle! It boils the water for tea."
  2. The rule, same words every time: "the kettle gets VERY hot. Hot, don’t touch — grown-ups only."
  3. Teach the pose: "hands behind your back… one big step back. That is the safety pose!"
  4. The job: "you are the safety checker — when the kettle whistles, you tell everyone: HOT!"
  5. Live demo (from the pose): the whistle, the steam, the announcement. The rule just became the child’s.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "kettle" sits over a gray stovetop kettle — spout ready, the whistle about to happen.

Ask your child

"What does the kettle do?" (boils water) "Is the kettle hot?" (VERY) "Show me the safety pose!" "Who uses the kettle?" (grown-ups)

What your child can say or do

Your child might snap into the safety pose at every whistle, referee visitors ("hot! step back!"), or request the tea ceremony after — the rule, loud and proud.

Out in the real world

Kettles whistle and steam in kitchens worldwide. Every sighting is a pose moment — "the kettle is hot!" — and the pattern quietly covers the stove, the oven and the BBQ.

Try it together

Safety Drill: the toy kettle "boils" (a whistle of cheeks), and the whole family snaps into the pose. Drills daily; the rule never fades.

Understanding check

Ask: "Is the kettle hot?" (VERY!) "What do we do?" (hands back, step back) "Who is the safety checker?" (me!)

Staying safe

The kettle’s water boils at 100 degrees and its steam burns too — both are grown-up territory. Rule: hot, don’t touch, grown-ups only; the child’s job is the safety pose and the announcement.

This lesson pairs with the Kettle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Kitchen Timer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the kitchen timer as the most useful card in the set: waiting has an end, numbers count something real, and the DING is a celebration every time.

What is this?

A kitchen timer is the round dial that counts down the minutes — cookies, tidy-ups, five-more-minutes — and ends every wait with a bell.

What does it mean?

The timer teaches that waiting is countable: the dial shrinks, the DING arrives. A child who owns the dial stops asking "is it ready YET?" — the timer says it first.

What does the child need to know?

You need the timer and the dial job: the child turns it to the number (with a grown-up’s eye), the household obeys the DING. Never overrule the bell — the timer’s authority is the whole magic.

Why this matters

Transitions with a bell are gentler than transitions with a debate. The timer makes endings fair, and fair endings get accepted.

What it teaches

Number-to-meaning (12 minutes = a real thing), time awareness, waiting tolerance, and the ritual authority of a shared bell.

Words to learn

kitchen timerdialminutestickDINGready

Say this to your child

“"Kitchen timer! The cookies need twelve minutes — set the dial… tick, tick, tick… DING! TIME! The cookies are ready. The timer says when — and when it dings, everyone listens!"”

Step by step

  1. Meet the dial: "kitchen timer! Turn it to the number… tick, tick, tick… DING!"
  2. The cookie job: "the cookies need twelve minutes. Set the dial!" (Guide the hand; the child turns.)
  3. The wait: listen for the ticks. "Can you hear it working?"
  4. The DING: celebrate like a goal — "TIME! Cookies ready!" Open the oven only now.
  5. The expansion: timers for tidy-ups (ten-minute games), turns (five more minutes), anything with an end. The bell rules them all.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "kitchen timer" sit over a round dial timer — numbers round the face, the pointer waiting for its wind-up.

Ask your child

"What does the timer count?" (the minutes) "What do we hear while it works?" (tick tick) "What happens at the end?" (DING — time!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might set timers for everything (hand-washing, bedtime, "five more slides"), or sprint to the oven at the DING — the dial, in charge.

Out in the real world

Timers live everywhere: the phone, the oven clock, the classroom bell. "Same as your kitchen timer!" connects every bell in the child’s life.

Try it together

Beat the Bell: tidy-up challenges against the timer — can the blocks be home before the DING? The bell becomes the teammate, not the enemy.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the timer do?" (counts down) "What do we hear?" (tick tick!) "What does DING mean?" (time — ready!)

This lesson pairs with the Kitchen Timer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Ladle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the ladle in two sittings: the cold practice where pouring is free, then the real serving where the child feeds the family and earns the thank-yous.

What is this?

A ladle is the long-handled deep spoon that scoops soup from pot to bowl — and the tool that puts a child in the host’s seat at dinner.

What does it mean?

Ladling is a full command course: dip depth, fill control, steady carry, targeted pour. It is also the job that earns thank-yous — and thank-yous are fuel.

What does the child need to know?

You need the ladle, cold soup or water for the sink practice, and the four-word sequence: dip… fill… carry… pour. Warm-not-hot soup is the promotion.

Why this matters

Serving others is the rare chore that comes with applause built in. Every bowl served lands a "thank you" — and a child with thanks coming keeps ladling.

What it teaches

Dip-and-fill control, steady carrying (the walk matters), targeted pouring, counting servings, and host pride.

Words to learn

ladlescoopdippourservethank you

Say this to your child

“"Ladle! The big deep spoon. Dip in the soup… fill it up… carry it steady… POUR — one bowl, served! Now everyone: dip, fill, pour! One for daddy, one for grandma… and one for YOU. Thank you, chef!"”

Step by step

  1. Meet the deep spoon: "ladle! The soup scooper — see the deep bowl on the handle?"
  2. Sink practice with cold soup: "dip… fill… carry… POUR into the bowl. No drips — steady hands!"
  3. Repeat until the pour is confident: bowls lined up, one fill per bowl.
  4. The promotion: warm (not hot) soup at dinner — the child ladles each bowl, counting: "one for daddy… one for grandma… one for ME!"
  5. The applause: thank-yos collected, the ladle washed and hung by its newest expert.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "ladle" sits over a green-handled ladle, its deep bowl up — ready for the dip that starts every serve.

Ask your child

"What does the ladle do?" (scoops and serves) "Show me dip… fill… pour!" "Who got your soup tonight?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might serve every meal, count the bowls aloud, or ladle the bath toys (transfer of skills) — the host, seated.

Out in the real world

Ladles work every soup pot, punch bowl and stew night. Each one is a hiring opportunity: "a ladle — the serving job is yours!"

Try it together

Soup Kitchen: bowls for every teddy, one ladle, cold water "soup" — fill each order, count the customers. Service with a smile, math with a ladle.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the ladle do?" (serves soup) "What are the four words?" (dip, fill, carry, pour) "Who says thank you?" (everyone!)

This lesson pairs with the Ladle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Measuring Cup — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the measuring cup as numbers doing a job: pour slow, watch the milk climb, stop at the line — the clearest early-numbers practice outside a workbook.

What is this?

A measuring cup is the clear jug with the marked lines — it counts the milk and water for a recipe, and the lines are numbers a child can watch working.

What does it mean?

Measuring is reading, maths and pouring control in one job. Eye-level reading of the line is even a real science skill (parallax) — learned now over a jug of milk.

What does the child need to know?

You need the jug, the milk and a level surface. The script: "set it down… crouch to the lines… pour SLOW… stop at the line!" The recipe decides the number; the child finds it.

Why this matters

A cake that rises because the milk was measured exactly is the best maths reward ever baked. Numbers with consequences get remembered.

What it teaches

Number recognition with meaning, slow-pour control, eye-level reading, and the measure-then-mix sequence that all recipes share.

Words to learn

measuring cuplinespourstopmilkexactly

Say this to your child

“"Measuring cup! Pour the milk in… SLOW… watch it climb the lines… closer… closer… STOP at the line! Crouch and look — eye level. Did we make it? One cup of milk, exactly. That is measuring!"”

Step by step

  1. Meet the lines: "measuring cup! The numbers on the side count the milk."
  2. Set the stage: "jug on the table — flat and still."
  3. The crouch: "come down to the lines — eye level! Now pour… SLOW…"
  4. The approach: "watch the milk climb… closer… STOP at the line!" Check together: "did we reach it? A drop more… STOP."
  5. The delivery: measured milk into the real recipe — "the cake knows you measured. It will rise happy."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "measuring cup" sit over a glass jug with its markings — the numbers, printed and patient.

Ask your child

"Where do the numbers live?" (on the jug) "How do we pour?" (slow!) "When do we stop?" (at the line!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might announce measurements for everything ("that is TWO lines of juice!"), pour with surgical slow-motion, or crouch to check like a scientist — numbers, working.

Out in the real world

Measuring jugs live in every baking kitchen; bath cups have lines too. "Line up the water — like your measuring cup!" finds numbers in bathtubs.

Try it together

Line Hunter: fill to one line, empty, fill to two, empty — a jug workout with counting in the middle. The reward: the measured milk goes in pancake batter.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do the lines do?" (measure) "How do we pour?" (slow, stop at the line) "How do we read it?" (eye level!)

This lesson pairs with the Measuring Cup flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Measuring Spoons — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the measuring spoons as precision at the smallest scale: find the size, scoop, level it flat, tip it in — five little scoops later, the cake knows the difference.

What is this?

The measuring spoons are the little green scoops on a ring — big, medium, small, tiny — that count the small things: sugar, salt, vanilla.

What does it mean?

Leveling is the secret skill: heaped and level spoons bake differently. The ring of sizes also invites ordering biggest-to-smallest — a free sorting game on the counter.

What does the child need to know?

You need the ring of spoons and the three-beat job: find the size the recipe names… scoop… LEVEL it flat with a finger… tip it in. The child is the spoon-keeper.

Why this matters

Small measures carry big consequences — salt especially. A child who levels a half-teaspoon correctly is doing chemistry with a spoon.

What it teaches

Size ordering, finger-leveling (fine motor), following recipe numbers, and the care that precision asks for.

Words to learn

measuring spoonssizesscooplevelflatpinch

Say this to your child

“"Measuring spoons! The little scoops on a ring. The recipe wants one teaspoon… find it… scoop… LEVEL it flat — drag your finger… flat as a pond! Tip it in. Small spoons, exact amounts — that is baking!"”

Step by step

  1. Meet the ring: "measuring spoons! Big… medium… small… tiny — all on one ring."
  2. The order game: line them up biggest to smallest. "The family, in a row!"
  3. The recipe call: "it wants ONE teaspoon of sugar — find it!"
  4. The scoop-and-level: "scoop… now level it flat — drag your finger across. Flat as a pond!"
  5. Tip it in and repeat for every small measure. The ring goes back on its hook, expert-worn.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "measuring spoons" sit over the green scoop set on its ring — nested sizes, ready to be fanned out.

Ask your child

"Which spoon is biggest?" "What does leveling do?" (makes it exact) "Find the teaspoon!"

What your child can say or do

Your child might wear the ring like keys, level everything (sugar, sand, patience), or correct a heaped spoon — precision, personal.

Out in the real world

Tiny measures appear in every recipe and medicine cup. "Level it flat — like your spoons!" scales the skill to cups and spoons for life.

Try it together

Size Parade: order the spoons, hide one, guess the missing size, repeat. The ring is a puzzle, a lesson and a toy — all legal.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do measuring spoons do?" (count small amounts) "What is the secret?" (level it flat!) "Order them — biggest to smallest!"

This lesson pairs with the Measuring Spoons flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Microwave — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the microwave with a job, not a ban: the child is the beep-watcher, the grown-up works the buttons, and the hot plate rule lands where it matters.

What is this?

A microwave is the white box that heats food fast — grown-up buttons, beeping finish, and a plate that comes out hot enough to matter.

What does it mean?

The microwave’s two rules — grown-ups operate, plates get hot — are the stove’s rules in smaller form. A child who waits for the beep has learned to wait for heat to cool.

What does the child need to know?

You need the machine and the ritual: food in (grown-up), buttons (grown-up), then the child’s job — the beep-watch: "BEEP! It’s ready!" The door’s steam gets one more step back.

Why this matters

A job satisfies the curiosity that buttons invite. The beep-watcher participates in every microwave meal without touching a single control.

What it teaches

Waiting tolerance, sound-cue response, the hot-plate rule, and steam awareness (the door opens OUT and the steam comes out too).

Words to learn

microwavebuttonsbeepreadyhot platesteam

Say this to your child

“"Microwave! In goes the plate… beep beep… the numbers count down. YOUR job: the beep! …BEEP! It’s ready! The plate inside is hot — grown-ups lift it out. Steam — step back. Teamwork dinner!"”

Step by step

  1. Name the box: "microwave! The quick-heat machine."
  2. The division: "grown-ups do the food and the buttons. YOUR job — the beep!"
  3. The wait: the child watches the countdown. "How many numbers left?"
  4. The announcement: BEEP — "BEEP! It’s ready!" (The job, delivered.)
  5. The plate rule: "the plate inside is HOT. Grown-ups take it out. Steam comes out too — one step back." Meal served by the full team.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "microwave" sits over a white countertop microwave — door shut, buttons waiting, countdown about to run.

Ask your child

"Who presses the buttons?" (grown-ups) "What is YOUR job?" (the beep!) "What is hot after the beep?" (the plate!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might count down the last ten seconds aloud, claim every beep ("MY job!"), or warn guests about steam — the watcher, promoted.

Out in the real world

Microwaves hum in kitchens, break rooms and holiday flats. Same ritual everywhere: "beep — that is MY job!" The rule travels by sound.

Try it together

Kitchen Radio: the microwave’s countdown is the show — numbers called, beep predicted, celebration scored. Waiting becomes a spectator sport.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who presses the buttons?" (grown-ups) "What do we wait for?" (the BEEP!) "What is hot afterwards?" (the plate — and the steam!)

Staying safe

The plate inside is scalding after the beep, and steam bursts out when the door opens. Rule: buttons and plates are grown-ups’; the child’s job is the beep-watch, one step back for the steam.

This lesson pairs with the Microwave flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Mixing Bowl — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the mixing bowl as the throne of every little helper: wide walls catch spills, hold steady, and give small arms room for big stirs.

What is this?

A mixing bowl is the big cream bowl with the green stripe — where flour meets milk meets eggs, and everything worth stirring happens.

What does it mean?

The big bowl is safety gear in disguise: wide walls catch spills, the base holds steady, and the scale fits a child’s enthusiasm. Naming it gives the job an address.

What does the child need to know?

You need the bowl on a damp cloth (the anti-slide trick) and the pour ritual: each ingredient lands with its name — "flour IN! milk IN!" The bowl catches everything.

Why this matters

A named bowl with a no-slide trick turns the messiest stage of baking into the calmest: everything lands IN the bowl, and the bowl does not move.

What it teaches

Pouring accuracy, the damp-cloth physics (friction!), ingredient vocabulary, and the before-after idea: empty bowl, then full.

Words to learn

mixing bowlbatterpour indamp clothsteadyfull

Say this to your child

“"Mixing bowl! The big, big bowl — on its damp cloth, steady and ready. Flour IN… milk IN… eggs IN! Everything lands in the bowl. Now stir, stir — the bowl holds it all. No spills! The batter’s home is happy."”

Step by step

  1. Set the throne: "mixing bowl! On its damp cloth — see? It will not slide."
  2. The pours, named: "flour IN… sugar IN… milk IN… eggs IN!" Each landing announced.
  3. The state check: "look — EMPTY bowl at the start. FULL bowl now. The bowl holds everything."
  4. Hand over to the spoon: "stir! The bowl is yours." (See the cooking-spoon lesson.)
  5. The finish: bowl scraped clean — "not one drop wasted. Wash the throne!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "mixing bowl" sit over a cream bowl with a green stripe — wide, deep and waiting for its ingredients.

Ask your child

"What lives in the mixing bowl?" (the batter) "Why the damp cloth?" (so it will not slide) "What was the bowl at the start?" (empty — now FULL!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might demand the big bowl for every mix, park it on its cloth unprompted, or guard the pour — the throne, respected.

Out in the real world

Big bowls mix everywhere: birthday cakes, pancake Sundays, the salad at grandma’s. Each one is a throne: "a mixing bowl — the batter’s home!"

Try it together

Bowl Balance: test the damp-cloth trick — bowl on bare table (slides!) vs bowl on cloth (steady!). Physics, demonstrated in one push.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does batter live?" (the mixing bowl) "What stops it sliding?" (the damp cloth) "What happens in the bowl?" (everything lands in!)

This lesson pairs with the Mixing Bowl flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Mortar and Pestle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the mortar and pestle as the oldest tool on the shelf: seeds go in, circles grind, powder comes out — the same way people have eaten for thousands of years.

What is this?

A mortar and pestle is the stone bowl and its grinding club — crush herbs and seeds the ancient way, long before anyone plugged anything in.

What does it mean?

The Ages 6+ cards are what-is-this cards — and this one is history: the tool fed the pharaohs. Fresh-ground smell vs jar smell is the demonstration that wins.

What does the child need to know?

You need the mortar, a few peppercorns or dried herbs, and grown-up hands guiding the first circles. The child’s jobs: hold, watch, smell, compare.

Why this matters

Understanding that food did not always come pre-ground — someone crushed it — is a history lesson a six-year-old can hold in one hand.

What it teaches

Historical thinking (old tools, same needs), grinding motion, sensory comparison (fresh vs jar), and patience — grinding is slow on purpose.

Words to learn

mortarpestlegrindseedspowderancient

Say this to your child

“"Mortar and pestle! Seeds in the stone bowl… grind, grind, in circles… press down… POWDER! People have done this for thousands of years. And the smell — sniff! Fresh-ground woke up. The jar is still asleep."”

Step by step

  1. Meet the pair: "mortar and pestle! The stone bowl and the club — the oldest kitchen tool there is."
  2. The story: "people used these thousands of years ago — no plugs, no buttons. Just circles."
  3. The demo, hands together: peppercorns in… "grind, grind, in circles… press down…"
  4. The reveal: powder! "the seeds became spice."
  5. The smell-off: fresh-ground vs jar — "sniff both. Which one woke up?" Fresh wins; the child just proved a theorem.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "mortar and pestle" sit over a stone bowl with its grinding club resting in it — heavy, carved, unhurried.

Ask your child

"What goes in the bowl?" (seeds and herbs) "What do we do?" (grind in circles!) "How old is this tool?" (thousands of years!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might grind rice with total focus, demand the smell-off at every meal, or explain the tool to guests — history, held.

Out in the real world

Mortars grind in spice markets, chemists’ shops and grandma’s cupboard. Each stone bowl is a meeting: "the ancient grinder!"

Try it together

Spice Museum: mortar, rolling pin, jar — three ways to crush, ranked by age. The mortar wins (and gets used). History with a smell test.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the pestle do?" (grinds) "What comes out?" (powder!) "How long have people used this?" (thousands of years!)

Staying safe

Stone is heavy and grinding is slow: grown-up hands guide or own the pestle. The child’s seats are holding the mortar steady, watching the circles and running the smell-off.

This lesson pairs with the Mortar and Pestle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Mug — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the mug with its two rules built in: mugs are for WARM drinks (grown-ups pour), and the carry is two hands, walk slow, set down before you sip.

What is this?

A mug is the big cream cup with the handle — the grown-up cup, and the promotion every child waits for: a real mug of warm cocoa, carried and sipped alone.

What does it mean?

The mug card carries its own safety line: warm drinks only, grown-ups pour. The two-hand carry rule transfers to every jug, bowl and cup the child will ever move — spill physics, learned gently.

What does the child need to know?

You need a child-size mug of WARM (never hot) cocoa and the script: "two hands around… walk slow… set it down… then sip." The sip comes after the landing.

Why this matters

Being trusted with a real mug is a promotion kids feel in their chest. The rules are the price of the promotion — and they are the same rules that protect every future cup.

What it teaches

Handle grip and two-hand carry, walking-with-liquid control, the hot-warm distinction, and the table manners of a cup with a saucer’s dignity.

Words to learn

mughandlewarmtwo handswalk slowsip

Say this to your child

“"Mug! The big cup with the handle. Two hands around it… walk slow… set it down… NOW sip. Mugs are for warm drinks — cocoa, warm milk — and grown-ups pour. You carry like a pro!"”

Step by step

  1. Present the promotion: "mug! The big cup — today YOU carry it."
  2. The pour (grown-up): "warm cocoa — warm, never hot. Grown-ups pour the mug."
  3. The carry: "two hands around the mug… walk slow… eyes on the cocoa."
  4. The landing: "set it down on the table… THERE. Now sip!" Sip after landing, every time.
  5. The repeat: mugs every cocoa night. The rules become the child’s own.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "mug" sits over a cream mug, handle out — the classic silhouette of every warm drink ever enjoyed.

Ask your child

"What drinks live in a mug?" (warm ones — cocoa!) "Who pours?" (grown-ups) "Show me the carry!" (two hands, slow)

What your child can say or do

Your child might request "mug cocoa" nightly, carry with breath-held concentration, or referee everyone’s grips — the promotion, honoured.

Out in the real world

Mugs hang in every kitchen and sit on every desk. Each one is a future promotion: "one day, a mug that size — first, master yours."

Try it together

Cocoa Ceremony: mugs, a small pot of warm cocoa, the full ritual — pour, carry, land, sip, sigh. Attendance mandatory; dignity guaranteed.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is a mug for?" (warm drinks) "How many hands carry it?" (two) "Sip before or after landing?" (after — always!)

This lesson pairs with the Mug flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Oven Mitt — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the oven mitt in two acts: the puppet show that makes it a friend, then the real lesson — heat travels, the mitt blocks it.

What is this?

An oven mitt is the thick quilted glove that stops heat — slide it on and even a hot tray can be carried. It looks like a puppet and works like a shield.

What does it mean?

Children who understand the mitt’s job respect hot things MORE, not less — because now they know exactly what heat does and exactly what stops it. The WHY is the whole lesson.

What does the child need to know?

You need the mitts and two stages: the puppet show (mitts say hello, high-five) and the mitt parade — mitt on, both hands, slow walk, oven to counter.

Why this matters

A rule without a why gets tested; a rule with a why gets kept. "Heat travels — the mitt blocks it" is a why a four-year-old can run experiments on for years.

What it teaches

Heat-and-protection thinking, two-hand coordination, slow-careful movement under load, and the safety-gear habit (helmets and mitts are cousins).

Words to learn

oven mittgloveheathot trayblockparade

Say this to your child

“"Oven mitt! The thick, puffy glove. Hello, mitt! And here is your job: the mitt stops the HEAT. Hot tray? The mitt says no — heat cannot get through! Mitt on… tray out… slow walk… safe. The oven-to-counter parade!"”

Step by step

  1. The puppet show: mitts on both your hands — "hello! We are the mitts!" High-fives, waving, voices. The glove is now a friend.
  2. The job reveal: "the mitt has a real job — it stops the HEAT. Hot tray? The mitt says no."
  3. The why: "heat travels — from the tray into everything it touches. The mitt is too thick. The heat cannot get through."
  4. The parade (grown-up): mitts on, oven open, tray out, slow walk to the rack — narrated: "mitt… tray… slow walk… safe!"
  5. The try-on: the child wears a mitt for a COOL tray — the fit, the feel, the readiness. Someday the tray will be theirs.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "oven mitt" sit over a green quilted glove — stitched, puffy and built for the parade it stars in.

Ask your child

"What does the mitt stop?" (the heat!) "Why is it thick?" (heat cannot get through) "Show me the mitt parade!" (mitt, tray, slow walk)

What your child can say or do

Your child might puppet-talk the mitts at every bake, explain the heat-travel idea to visitors, or demand parade tickets — the shield, understood.

Out in the real world

Mitts hang by every oven on Earth. Each one is a colleague: "the heat shield!" And the idea scales — bike helmets, oven gloves, pot holders: safety gear everywhere.

Try it together

Mitt Theatre: both mitts, a full puppet show for the teddies, followed by the parade narrated by the child. Safety and show business, same glove.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the mitt stop?" (heat) "Why?" (too thick — it cannot get through) "Show me the parade!"

Staying safe

The mitt protects the wearer, not the curious: only the glove’s owner touches the hot tray. The child’s mitt moments are cool trays and puppet shows until hands grow steadier.

This lesson pairs with the Oven Mitt flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Peeler — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the peeler as a look-and-learn tool: the ribbons are the show, the hidden blade is the rule, and the carrot’s skin finally has a destination.

What is this?

A peeler is the green swivel tool that takes the skin off carrots and potatoes in long ribbons — its edge is sharp even though it looks tiny.

What does it mean?

The peeler looks harmless and is not — exactly why it is a great sharp-things teacher. And watching peels curl off answers a question most adults never think to answer: where does the skin GO?

What does the child need to know?

You need the peeler in the drawer, a carrot for the grown-up demo and the rule: "the edge is sharp even when it looks small — grown-ups peel." The child’s jobs: find it, watch, collect the ribbons.

Why this matters

Watching peels curl is the demonstration; collecting them for compost or soup closes the loop. Respect learned by looking, at six, is the safe introduction.

What it teaches

Tool taxonomy (looks small, behaves sharp), the skin-to-compost loop, swivel-blade observation, and patience for someday-hands.

Words to learn

peelerskinribbonsswivelsharpgrown-ups

Say this to your child
