“"Peeler! It slides down the carrot — swish! Long ribbons of skin fall off. Careful: the blade is sharp and hidden. Grown-ups peel — you collect the ribbons! And the ribbons go… to the compost! Not rubbish — soup food."”

Step by step

  1. Drawer meeting: "peeler! The skin remover — find it together."
  2. Open and close gently (grown-up fingers on the blade end): "the blade swivels — it follows the carrot’s curves."
  3. The demo: grown-up peels — "swish… long ribbons of skin!" The child collects them.
  4. The rule, same words: "the edge is SHARP even when it looks tiny. Grown-ups peel; kids watch the ribbons."
  5. The loop: ribbons to the compost or the soup pot — "the skin is not rubbish. The soup wants it."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "peeler" sits over a green vegetable peeler — swivel head, thin body, the smallest sharp thing in the drawer.

Ask your child

"What does the peeler do?" (removes skin) "Is the blade sharp?" (yes — even though it looks small!) "Where do the ribbons go?" (compost or soup!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might collect ribbons at every peel, correct the record ("the blade is sharp!"), or request soup with "the carrot ribbons" — the loop, owned.

Out in the real world

Peelers ride in every kitchen drawer and camping kit. Each one gets the nod: "sharp ribbon-maker — grown-ups peel." The rule packs light.

Try it together

Compost Race: peel one carrot (grown-up), then sort the ribbons — compost bowl or soup pot? The child decides, delivers and reports. The loop, run by the smallest official.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the peeler remove?" (the skin) "Is it sharp?" (yes — hidden and sharp) "Who peels?" (grown-ups — me someday!)

Staying safe

The peeler’s blade is sharp and hidden — it scrapes more surprised fingers than knives. Rule: grown-ups peel; the child finds, watches and collects. Hands grow into it years from now.

This lesson pairs with the Peeler flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Plate — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the plate as the host’s tool: one plate per seat, handed out with ceremony, counted as they land — and the empty plate’s trip to the sink ends the job.

What is this?

A plate is the round cream plate with the green rim where dinner lands — and setting the table is the first hosting job a child can fully own.

What does it mean?

A named plate gives a child ownership of their own eating space — picky eaters often accept food on "their" plate that they reject off it. And counting plates per seat is early maths at dinner speed.

What does the child need to know?

You need the plates and the seat map: "one for daddy… one for grandma… one for YOU." The child sets; the family arrives. The sink delivery is the finish line.

Why this matters

A table set by the child makes the child part of the meal before the food lands — membership changes eating behaviour more than any bribe.

What it teaches

One-to-one matching (plate to seat), counting with purpose, carrying-with-two-hands care, and the host identity that sets tables for life.

Words to learn

plateset the tableseatcountemptysink

Say this to your child

“"Plate! One for daddy… one for grandma… one for YOU! Count the seats — everyone has a plate. The table is SET. And after dinner: empty plates to the sink, two hands, job done. What a host!"”

Step by step

  1. The job briefing: "plates! Tonight YOU set the table."
  2. The map: "how many seats? Count them… four! How many plates? Four — one each!"
  3. The handout, with ceremony: "daddy’s plate… grandma’s plate… YOUR plate." Each landing named.
  4. The gap check: "did everyone get one? A seat with no plate? Fix it, host!"
  5. The finish: after dinner, "empty plates to the sink — carry with two hands!" The job closes; the host bows.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "plate" sits over a cream plate with a green rim — round, ready and waiting for dinner’s landing.

Ask your child

"How many seats tonight?" "Whose plate is this?" "Where do empty plates go?" (the sink!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might count the family nightly, correct a missing plate, or refuse to eat off any plate but "mine" — the host, seated at their own table.

Out in the real world

Plates stack in every cupboard and queue at every buffet. "One per seat" scales to picnics, parties and restaurants — the host’s rule is universal.

Try it together

Restaurant Night: menus, orders (real food), and the child sets every place before cooking starts. The tip is a thank-you; the repeat customers are guaranteed.

Understanding check

Ask: "What lands on the plate?" (dinner!) "How many plates per seat?" (one) "What do we do after?" (sink — two hands!)

This lesson pairs with the Plate flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Refrigerator — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the refrigerator as the kitchen’s landmark: every food conversation starts there — milk, yogurt, apples — and the cold is the WHY that explains it all.

What is this?

A refrigerator is the big gray two-door cupboard that hums — it keeps food cold so it stays good, and it is the most-visited appliance in the house.

What does it mean?

The fridge teaches the why of cold: food goes bad when warm, cold slows the going-bad, the fridge is the cold cupboard. One little science story explains a hundred dinner mysteries.

What does the child need to know?

You need the fridge and the find-it game: "bring me the milk… find the cheese… where do the eggs live?" Plus the door rule: one open, one close.

Why this matters

A child who knows where food lives can help with every meal, find their own snacks and understand the shopping list — the fridge is infrastructure for independence.

What it teaches

Food-to-place mapping, the cold-preservation idea, door discipline, and the food vocabulary that every meal after this one uses.

Words to learn

refrigeratorfridgecoldmilkfreshclose the door

Say this to your child

“"Refrigerator! The big, cold fridge — brrr! The milk lives here, the cheese here, the apples in the drawer. The fridge keeps our food cold so it stays fresh — that is why it hums! One open… one close. The cold stays in!"”

Step by step

  1. Open the landmark: "refrigerator! The big cold cupboard — brrr!"
  2. The tour: "the milk lives here… the yogurt here… the apples in the drawer." Name homes, not just foods.
  3. The game: "bring me the milk! Find the cheese!" Each fetch lands the mapping deeper.
  4. The why: "food goes bad when it is warm. The fridge keeps it COLD — so it stays fresh. That is why it hums all day: it is working!"
  5. The rule: "one open… one close. The cold stays in when the door is shut." Mission complete.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "refrigerator" sits over a gray two-door refrigerator — handles out, hum on, the kitchen’s coldest resident.

Ask your child

"Where does the milk live?" "Why is the fridge cold?" (to keep the food fresh) "What is the door rule?" (one open, one close!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might fetch requested foods proudly, explain the hum ("it is working!"), or police doors all evening — the cold cupboard, guarded.

Out in the real world

Fridges hum in every home, shop and holiday flat. Same mapping everywhere: "where does the milk live HERE?" The game travels.

Try it together

Fridge Map: draw the shelves, place paper "foods" on the drawing, then find the real ones. Map to machine — the full tour, run by the smallest guide.

Understanding check

Ask: "What keeps the food cold?" (the refrigerator) "Why cold?" (so it stays fresh!) "What do we do with the door?" (one open, one close)

This lesson pairs with the Refrigerator flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Rolling Pin — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the rolling pin as the baking job with the lowest stakes and the highest sensory payoff: cool dough, dusty flour, the slow squash of the pin.

What is this?

A rolling pin is the wooden roller with the green handles — it flattens dough for cookies and pies, and rolling it well is a real two-hand skill.

What does it mean?

Rolling is two-hand coordination, pressure control and patience — the whole upper body works. And the score is visible: an even sheet, ready for cutters.

What does the child need to know?

You need flour on the counter, dough divided (one piece per roller) and the technique: "hold both handles… LONG pushes… edge to edge… turn the dough, roll again."

Why this matters

Uneven cookies taste exactly the same — which keeps the joy safe while the skill grows. Bakers are made at the rolling-pin stage.

What it teaches

Two-hand coordination, pressure modulation, the turn-and-roll rhythm, and sensory tolerance for sticky, floury, squishy work.

Words to learn

rolling pindoughrollflatfloureven

Say this to your child

“"Rolling pin! Hold both handles… push — roll, roll, roll! To the edge… and back. Turn the dough… roll again. Flat as a pancake! Now the cookie cutters — stamp, stamp! Your dough, your cookies. Uneven ones taste just as good."”

Step by step

  1. Flour the stage: "sprinkle sprinkle — the flour keeps the dough from sticking."
  2. Divide: "one piece for you, one for me — bakers’ fair share."
  3. The technique: "both handles… long pushes… roll to the edge and back. Now turn the dough… roll again!"
  4. The check: "is it even? Thick side? Roll there… FLAT as a pancake!"
  5. The reward: cookie cutters stamp out the shapes — "your dough, your cookies." Uneven ones taste identical; everyone knows.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "rolling pin" sit over a wooden pin with green handles — flour-dusted in every kitchen it has ever visited.

Ask your child

"What does the pin do?" (flattens dough) "Show me a long push!" "What do we do when one side is thick?" (turn and roll there)

What your child can say or do

Your child might roll everything (playdough counts), demand their own dough piece, or check flatness with two fingers — the baker, rolling.

Out in the real world

Rolling pins flatten in every bakery and grandma’s kitchen. Each one is a handshake: "same as yours — now roll!"

Try it together

Dough Bar: playdough and real dough stations — roll flat, cut shapes, compare thicknesses. The bar serves both crafts and both cooks.

Understanding check

Ask: "What rolls the dough?" (the rolling pin) "How do we hold it?" (both handles) "What is the goal?" (flat — even!)

This lesson pairs with the Rolling Pin flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Saucepan — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the saucepan with the hot rule and its antidote: the real pot is untouchable, the pretend pot at the play table takes the reaching away.

What is this?

A saucepan is the silver pot with the long handle that makes soup, pasta and porridge — and it lives on the stove, in the hot, don’t-touch family.

What does it mean?

Hot pan plus short person plus reaching hand is the classic kitchen accident — so this card names the pot, rehearses the rule and ALWAYS offers the safe twin: a toy pot at the play table.

What does the child need to know?

You need the rule ("the pot is hot — step back"), the habit (handles turned inward) and the play-table pot where the same meal gets "cooked" by the child.

Why this matters

The pretend pot is not a consolation prize — it is the safety design. Reaching hands have a legal target; the real pot keeps its distance.

What it teaches

Hot-zone awareness, the handle-inward habit (spatial), pretend-cooking sequences, and the rule-with-a-voice pattern that generalizes.

Words to learn

saucepanpotstovehotstep backpretend pot

Say this to your child

“"Saucepan! The soup pot on the stove. The pot gets VERY hot — the pot is hot, step back! Handles turn inward… no reaching. And YOUR pot is at the play table — stir, stir, cook the same soup! Two pots, two chefs, zero burns."”

Step by step

  1. Name the pot: "saucepan! The pot that cooks the soup."
  2. The rule, with its voice: "the saucepan sits on the stove and gets VERY hot. The pot is hot — step back!"
  3. The habit: "see the handle? We turn it INWARD — no reaching hands can find it."
  4. The twin: the toy pot at the play table — "you cook the same soup HERE! Spoon… stir… yummy."
  5. The split: the real pot bubbles untouched; the pretend pot runs the whole menu. Both cooks employed.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "saucepan" sits over a silver pot with its long handle — the handle shown exactly as it should sit: turned inward, away from small hands.

Ask your child

"What does the saucepan cook?" (soup, pasta!) "What do we say about the pot?" (hot — step back!) "Where is YOUR pot?" (the play table)

What your child can say or do

Your child might announce the rule at every simmer, turn toy handles inward, or serve pretend soup for hours — the twin kitchen, staffed.

Out in the real world

Pots simmer on every stove and campfire. Each one gets the call: "hot pot — step back!" The rule and the inward handle travel to every kitchen the child enters.

Try it together

Twin Kitchens: real dinner (grown-up pot) and play dinner (child pot) cook the SAME menu, course by course. The play pot serves the teddies; the reviews are glowing.

Understanding check

Ask: "Is the saucepan hot?" (VERY) "What do we do?" (step back!) "Where is the child’s pot?" (the play table!)

Staying safe

The saucepan and its handle carry boiling heat. Rule: the pot is grown-ups’ — the child’s pot is at the play table. Handles always turned inward; step back called by name.

This lesson pairs with the Saucepan flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Spatula — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the spatula through the flip: cold-pan practice until the wrist knows the move, then one real pancake flip — a breakfast legend retold for years.

What is this?

A spatula is the flat green turning tool that slides under pancakes and flips them — the tool every kid wants to hold on pancake morning.

What does it mean?

The flip is precision work — slide depth, lift speed, wrist turn. Practising on a cold pan removes every burn risk while keeping all the skill.

What does the child need to know?

You need the spatula, a cold pan and a piece of bread or foam pancake for practice. The real flip: pan off the heat for the moment, grown-up hand hovering, one attempt.

Why this matters

Cold-pan practice is honest rehearsal: the wrist learns exactly the motion it will need, with zero risk. The first real flip lands in family legend.

What it teaches

Slide-and-lift control, wrist rotation, timing patience (wait for the bubbles!), and the confidence of a practised skill landing.

Words to learn

spatulaflipslideliftwristpancake

Say this to your child

“"Spatula! The flat flipper. Slide it under… lift… and FLIP! Over it goes. Practise on the cold pan first — ten flips! A real pancake says when: wait for the bubbles… then flip. One flip, and you are a legend."”

Step by step

  1. Meet the flipper: "spatula! The flat tool that turns food over — both sides get cooked."
  2. Cold-pan school: bread in the cold pan — "slide UNDER… lift… and FLIP! Over it goes." Ten flips, no panic.
  3. The timing lesson: "a real pancake says when — bubbles pop in the middle, THEN flip."
  4. The real flip: pan off the heat, grown-up hovering — "your spatula… slide… lift… FLIP!"
  5. The legend: photo if allowed, retelling mandatory. "Remember when you flipped the pancake?"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "spatula" sits over a green turning spatula — flat blade, angled handle, built for the slide-under.

Ask your child

"What does the spatula do?" (flips food) "Show me the flip on the cold pan!" "When does a real pancake flip?" (when the bubbles pop!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might flip toast (gently), narrate bubble-watching at breakfast, or retell the flip at dinner — the legend, growing.

Out in the real world

Spatulas flip in every kitchen and burger van. Each sighting is a nod: "a flipper — yours is at home, ready."

Try it together

Flip Trials: cold-pan flips scored for style — gentle, bold, upside-down accident (also celebrated). Ten flips to graduate to pancake morning.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the spatula do?" (flips) "Where do we practise?" (the cold pan!) "What does a pancake say before the flip?" (bubbles!)

This lesson pairs with the Spatula flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Strainer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the strainer beside its cousin: same idea as the colander, finer net — demonstrated with a snowfall of icing sugar that no child forgets.

What is this?

A strainer is the fine mesh net on a handle — holes so small they catch flour lumps and tea leaves, letting only liquid slip through.

What does it mean?

Strainer and colander make a compare-and-contrast pair: same job, different hole size, different catches. Understanding "the mesh chooses what passes" is early engineering.

What does the child need to know?

You need both tools and a test: which catches flour? Which catches pasta? Then the showstopper — icing sugar shaken through the strainer: snowfall.

Why this matters

The pair teaches by difference: one tool, two hole sizes, two results. Children who can explain WHY the mesh works have engineering thinking — and icing-sugar snowfalls are unbeatable theater.

What it teaches

Comparative thinking (hole sizes), sift-and-strain vocabulary, fine observation, and the flour-lump problem-solving the sieve solves.

Words to learn

strainermeshfinesiftsnowfallcatch

Say this to your child

“"Strainer! The fine net with the handle — the colander’s careful cousin. Flour test: the colander lets it fall, the strainer CATCHES it. And the magic: tap tap tap — sugar SNOW on the cake! Same idea, finer holes."”

Step by step

  1. The cousins together: "strainer and colander — same idea! But look at the holes."
  2. The test: flour into each — "the colander lets it fall! The strainer catches it. The mesh is finer."
  3. The job: "the strainer catches lumps and seeds — only the smooth stuff passes."
  4. The showstopper: icing sugar in the strainer, tapped over a cake — "SNOW! The mesh makes sugar snow."
  5. The verdict: "same idea, finer net. Choose your tool by what you catch."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "strainer" sits over a fine-mesh sieve with a green handle — the mesh woven tight enough to catch a snowfall.

Ask your child

"What does the mesh catch?" (lumps, seeds, flour) "How is it different from the colander?" (finer holes!) "What does it make on the cake?" (sugar snow!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might sift everything (flour, sand, glitter requests), explain the mesh to guests, or request "snow cake" — the pair, understood.

Out in the real world

Strainers sift in tea cultures worldwide — and pools, and paint shops. "A mesh that chooses what passes" appears everywhere once named.

Try it together

Mesh Lab: strainer vs colander vs plate — flour, rice, water through each. Chart what passes, what stays. The lab report is a drawing; the scientist is five.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the strainer catch?" (the fine bits) "Who is its cousin?" (the colander) "What makes snow?" (icing sugar through the mesh!)

This lesson pairs with the Strainer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Toaster — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the toaster with its ceremony — bread in, lever CLUNK, wait, POP — and the rule said every time: only bread goes in the slots.

What is this?

A toaster is the gray box with two slots that turns bread into toast — and it comes with the kitchen’s most specific safety rule.

What does it mean?

The toaster teaches a routine AND the first "never put metal in it" rule that generalizes to every appliance. Toast is also the breakfast a three-year-old can help make from start to butter.

What does the child need to know?

You need bread, the lever (the child’s job, with a grown-up beside) and the rule, same words: "bread in, toast out, no fingers, no forks." The grown-up lifts the toast.

Why this matters

The lever-press job is deeply satisfying (CLUNK!) and keeps the child in the routine while the hot slots stay hands-off. The POP is the reward.

What it teaches

Routine sequencing, lever mechanics (push down, spring up), the metal-in-appliance rule, and breakfast independence.

Words to learn

toasterslotsleverpoptoastno forks

Say this to your child

“"Toaster! Bread goes in the slots… press the lever — CLUNK! Wait for it… POP! Toast jumps up! Grown-ups lift the toast — slots are hot. And the rule: only BREAD goes in the toaster. Never fingers, never forks!"”

Step by step

  1. Name the machine: "toaster! The toast machine."
  2. Bread in (child, grown-up beside): "one slice each slot — bread ONLY."
  3. The lever: "push it down — CLUNK! Now it gets warm inside."
  4. The wait and the POP: "watch… POP! Toast jumps up!" The grown-up lifts it out — "the slots are hot; grown-ups lift."
  5. The rule, every time: "only bread goes in the toaster — never fingers, never forks." Butter, eat, repeat tomorrow.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "toaster" sits over a gray two-slice toaster — slots up, lever waiting for its press.

Ask your child

"What goes in the slots?" (bread — only bread!) "Who presses the lever?" (me!) "What does the toaster say?" (POP!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might press levers everywhere (chair recliners count), quote the rule to visitors, or butter their own POP — breakfast, claimed.

Out in the real world

Toasters pop in kitchens worldwide. Same ritual, same rule: "CLUNK… wait… POP!" — and the slots stay bread-only for life.

Try it together

Toast Bar: bread choice, lever duty (supervised), butter spreading with the child knife, toppings bar. The full production line, staffed by the shortest chef.

Understanding check

Ask: "What goes in the slots?" (bread only!) "Who lifts the toast?" (grown-ups) "What does the lever do?" (CLUNK down — POP up!)

Staying safe

The slots are hot inside and stay hot after the POP. Rule: bread only — never fingers, never forks, never anything metal; the grown-up lifts the toast. The rule is said every single time.

This lesson pairs with the Toaster flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Tongs — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the tongs as fingers on sticks: the pom-pom relay builds the squeeze hand, and the salad-serving job puts it to delicious work.

What is this?

Tongs are the two green arms that grab — squeeze to open, release to close. They pick up food without fingers ever touching it.

What does it mean?

Tongs are a fine-motor classic: the open-squeeze rhythm builds hand strength better than most toys, disguised as a job. The grip is the exact muscle pattern pencils ask for later.

What does the child need to know?

You need the tongs, a bowl of pom-poms (or cotton balls) and a second bowl for the relay: squeeze open… grab… carry… release. Then the real job — serving salad.

Why this matters

Tools as extra fingers is a big idea — the whole secret of kitchens and workshops. Tongs are where a four-year-old discovers it.

What it teaches

Squeeze strength and control, open-release rhythm, targeted placement, and the tool-as-hand concept that tools everywhere will reuse.

Words to learn

tongssqueezegrabcarryreleaseserve

Say this to your child

“"Tongs! Squeeze to open… let go to grab! Move the pom-poms — squeeze, carry, release! Now the big job: serve the salad — tongs only, no fingers! Squeeze… serve… well done. Fingers on sticks!"”

Step by step

  1. Meet the arms: "tongs! Fingers that live on a stick. Squeeze to open… let go to grab!"
  2. The relay: "move the pom-poms — one squeeze at a time — bowl to bowl!" Count the transfers.
  3. The trick shot: the smallest pom-pom. Steady hands, slow squeeze, triumph.
  4. The promotion: salad at dinner — "serve the family, tongs only, no fingers allowed!"
  5. The bow: tongs washed, hung, and requested for every serving night after. The grip grows a writer.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "tongs" sits over a pair of green kitchen tongs, arms open — ready for the squeeze that starts every grab.

Ask your child

"How do tongs open?" (squeeze!) "What did you grab?" "Can fingers touch the salad?" (no — tongs only!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might tong everything (socks, toys, the cat’s toy — supervised), serve every salad, or teach a teddy the squeeze — the grip, everywhere.

Out in the real world

Tongs serve at buffets, barbecues and bakeries worldwide. Each pair is a gym: "squeeze grabs — like yours!"

Try it together

Tong Olympics: pom-pom relay, cotton-ball stacking, the marshmallow-and-cocoa service. Events scored; hand strength wins everything.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do tongs do?" (grab without fingers) "Show me squeeze-open!" "What do they build?" (hand strength — for writing!)

This lesson pairs with the Tongs flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Trash Bin — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the trash bin as mess’s destination: pedal opens the lid, in it goes, close. And the scraps-bowl job after dinner is the easiest real chore in the house.

What is this?

A trash bin is the gray pedal bin with the green lid — the place wrappers and peels go, operated by the best foot-button in the kitchen.

What does it mean?

A named bin gives mess an address — halving the "where does this go?" questions. The pedal works by foot, so hands stay clean and the lid feels like magic.

What does the child need to know?

You need the bin and the pedal-toss: step, open, in, close. Then the promotion: carrying the little scraps bowl after dinner — one trip, one job, owned.

Why this matters

Bin jobs scale perfectly: pedal-toss at two, scraps-bowl at three, bin-day carrying at five. The first chore in the house is a foot pedal away.

What it teaches

Foot-pedal coordination, aim-and-drop, the tidy-as-we-go habit, and chore pride that scales with the child.

Words to learn

trash binpedallidin it goesscrapstidy

Say this to your child

“"Trash bin! Step on the pedal — the lid opens! In it goes… close. You are the bin chief: wrappers, peels, paper — pedal, toss, close! And after dinner, the scraps bowl rides to the bin. Two hands. What a helper!"”

Step by step

  1. Demo the magic: "trash bin! Step on the pedal… the lid opens — whoosh! In it goes… close."
  2. The job title: "you are the bin chief — every wrapper goes in by YOUR pedal."
  3. The round: cooking wrappers, paper towels, apple skins — pedal, toss, close, each one named.
  4. The promotion: "after dinner, the scraps bowl goes to the bin — carry it with two hands!"
  5. The close: lid down, hands washed — "the bin chief keeps the kitchen clean!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "trash bin" sit over a gray pedal bin with a green lid — the pedal at the front, waiting for a small foot.

Ask your child

"Where do wrappers go?" (in the bin!) "What opens the lid?" (the pedal — your foot!) "Whose job is the scraps bowl?" (the bin chief — me!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might pedal-toss everything (sweet wrappers, hopes), carry the scraps bowl nightly, or refuse bins without pedals — the chore, claimed.

Out in the real world

Bins pedal and swing in every kitchen, park and classroom. "Where does this go? The bin!" scales to every mess the child will ever meet.

Try it together

Bin Hoops: soft wrappers tossed from a step back — pedal, aim, SCORE. Baskets counted; the kitchen tidies itself between quarters.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does mess go?" (the trash bin) "What opens the lid?" (the pedal) "What is the after-dinner job?" (the scraps bowl!)

This lesson pairs with the Trash Bin flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.

KITCHEN LESSON · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Whisk — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the whisk as instant cause and effect: effort in, foam out — the wrist circles are hard work, enormously satisfying, and writing will borrow them later.

What is this?

A whisk is the balloon-shaped beater that turns eggs fluffy and cream into clouds — the helper tool that feels the most like magic.

What does it mean?

Whisking builds wrist and forearm strength — the same motion writing asks for. And it shows cause and effect at top speed: whip harder, more bubbles, immediately.

What does the child need to know?

You need the whisk, three cracked eggs in the mixing bowl and the challenge: "bubbles in thirty seconds — GO!" The whipped eggs go straight to the pan for scrambled eggs.

Why this matters

A four-year-old who whisks the eggs never has to be asked to try them. Investment is the oldest flavour enhancer there is.

What it teaches

Wrist circles and forearm strength, sustained effort (thirty seconds is LONG), foam science (air in the eggs), and the pride-to-appetite pipeline.

Words to learn

whiskwhipbubblesfoamwristfluffy

Say this to your child

“"Whisk! Fast circles — whip whip whip! From the wrist… look, BUBBLES! The whisk put air in the eggs. More whip — more bubbles! And fluffy eggs for breakfast — whisked by YOU. Wrist of steel!"”

Step by step

  1. Meet the balloon: "whisk! The bouncy wire beater — hold the handle."
  2. The technique: "fast circles — from the WRIST, not the arm! Whip whip whip."
  3. The challenge: "bubbles in thirty seconds — go!" Count loudly; cheer the foam.
  4. The reveal: "LOOK — bubbles! The whisk put air in the eggs. Air makes them FLUFFY."
  5. The reward: eggs to the pan (grown-up sizzles), scrambled and served — "whisked by you. Fluffiest ever."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "whisk" sits over a balloon whisk with a black and green handle — wires round, ready for the circles.

Ask your child

"What does the whisk make?" (bubbles — foam!) "Where do the circles come from?" (the wrist!) "What do bubbles do to eggs?" (make them fluffy!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might whisk everything (pudding, bath, imagination), time their own bubble challenges, or demand fluffier eggs weekly — the wrist, strengthening.

Out in the real world

Whisks whip in every bakery and breakfast kitchen. Each one is a gym membership: "wrist circles — like yours!"

Try it together

Bubble Challenge League: thirty seconds, three rounds, bubble volume scored (visually!). Champions whisk the real eggs. Records fall weekly.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the whisk do?" (whips bubbles) "Where do circles come from?" (the wrist) "What does air do to eggs?" (fluffy!)

This lesson pairs with the Whisk flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kitchen Things.
